title: Pac-Man's four ghosts each hunt differently
hook: Each Pac-Man ghost follows its own simple rule, and together they feel alive.
peek: The four ghosts in Pac-Man look alike, but each one is steered by a different targeting rule. One chases, one ambushes, one works off a partner and one keeps losing interest. Those few lines of logic give them personalities.
lede: Pac-Man came out in Japan in 1980, designed by Toru Iwatani at Namco. The ghosts never see the whole maze. At each junction a ghost simply turns toward a target tile, and each ghost picks its target in a different way. That small difference is why Blinky, Pinky, Inky and Clyde seem to have moods of their own.

bullets.text: The red ghost aims straight at the tile Pac-Man is on. Late in each level, as the dots run low, he also speeds up, which is why players remember him as the relentless one.
The pink ghost aims at a spot four tiles ahead of Pac-Man, trying to cut him off. A quirk in the original code shifts that spot sideways when Pac-Man faces up, and expert players exploit it.

The cyan ghost uses both Pac-Man and Blinky. His target is found by drawing a line from Blinky to a point just ahead of Pac-Man and doubling it, so he can seem helpful one moment and erratic the next.
The orange ghost chases Pac-Man until he gets within about eight tiles, then turns back toward his home corner. Up close he wanders off, which makes him look shy or confused.
The ghosts do not hunt all the time. On a fixed timer they break off and head to their own four corners, then return to the chase. These pauses give players breathing room and a rhythm to learn.
